summary.text: A 64-year-old woman was admitted with gradually worsening dysphagia for half a year, able to take only fluids, from a large hard immobile left neck mass. She had been diagnosed with papillary thyroid cancer by cytopathology at a local hospital, and had no history of high blood pressure, diabetes, hyperthyroidism, autoimmune disease or family illness. Thyroglobulin was markedly raised while other thyroid hormone levels were normal.

Ultrasound showed a hypoechoic left neck mass without enlarged cervical or supraclavicular nodes, and core biopsy indicated classic papillary thyroid cancer. CT showed a 56 × 37 mm mass compressing the trachea and esophagus, with MRI, endoscopy and esophagram showing esophageal stenosis, compression and invasion. The multi-disciplinary team judged complete safe resection difficult and proposed preoperative apatinib.

Apatinib 500 mg orally once per day was started on February 14, 2019; mild hypertension was the only adverse drug reaction. One month later CT showed shrinkage to 36 × 25 mm and Tg fell to 861.20 ng/mL. After 6 weeks dysphagia remitted and CT showed 29 × 26 mm. After a 10-day withdrawal she underwent total thyroidectomy, left central lymph node dissection and esophageal muscular layer resection, with no esophageal fistula.

Postoperative pathology showed classic papillary thyroid cancer with capsular invasion, central lymph node metastasis in 1/2 nodes, pT4aN1aM0 stage III, and BRAF V600E and TERT C228T mutations. Tg fell to 4.80 ng/mL in the first month of follow-up; six months later imaging showed no pulmonary or bone metastasis, she received 100 mCi radioiodine ablation, and at one year Tg was 0.81 ng/mL with no recurrence or metastasis.
